title: Repent or Perish, a Woman Set Free, and the Narrow Door
summary: Told of Galileans killed by Pilate and of eighteen crushed by a falling tower, Jesus denies that the victims were worse sinners and calls his hearers to repent, then tells of a barren fig tree given one more year. On the Sabbath he frees a woman bent over for eighteen years, compares the kingdom to mustard seed and leaven, warns that many will find the narrow door shut, and, warned about Herod, laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.
story:
Chapter 12 ended with Jesus rebuking crowds who could read the weather but not the present time, and urging them to settle with their accuser on the way to court before it is too late (12:54-59). This chapter presses the same urgency from several sides. News of two disasters becomes a summons to repentance; a fig tree lives on borrowed time; the door of the master's house will not stay open forever. Between the warnings stands the healing of a woman bent double for eighteen years, a picture of what the kingdom does when it arrives: it releases those Satan has bound, and it does so on the Sabbath, the day of rest and release.

Luke reminds the reader in verse 22 that Jesus is still making his way toward Jerusalem, the destination set in 9:51, and the chapter ends there in spirit, with Jesus' lament over the city that kills the prophets. The chapter is framed by two rulers who kill: Pilate, who mixed Galilean blood with sacrifices (verse 1), and Herod Antipas, who wants to kill Jesus (verse 31). The two will meet again over Jesus in Luke 23, where they become friends on the day of his trial (23:12). Chapter 14 follows directly with another Sabbath healing at a Pharisee's table and a parable about a great banquet, taking up the feast of the kingdom promised in 13:29.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36. The killing of Galileans whose blood he mixed with their sacrifices is not recorded outside Luke, but it fits what other sources say of him. Josephus reports that Pilate brought military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem by night and backed down only when crowds lay down and bared their necks (Antiquities 18.55-59; War 2.169-174); that he took money from the temple treasury to build an aqueduct and, when crowds protested, sent soldiers dressed as civilians with hidden clubs among them, killing many (Antiquities 18.60-62; War 2.175-177); and that in AD 36 he attacked a crowd of Samaritans gathered at Mount Gerizim by a prophet who promised to show them vessels hidden by Moses, after which Vitellius, the legate of Syria, sent him to Rome to answer for it (Antiquities 18.85-89). Philo of Alexandria describes a quarrel over gilded shields Pilate set up in Herod's palace in Jerusalem (Embassy to Gaius 299-305). Attempts to identify Luke's incident with one of these, most often the aqueduct riot, are guesses; Luke's report stands on its own. Its detail about sacrifices places it in the temple courts, where ordinary Israelites slaughtered their own animals only at Passover (m. Pesahim 5:5-7 describes them doing so in three groups), so a Passover clash is the likeliest setting. Galileans had a reputation for rebellion: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census in AD 6 (Antiquities 18.1-10, 18.23; Acts 5:37).

The tower of Siloam is otherwise unknown. Siloam was the pool and district at the southern end of the old city of David, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel from the Gihon spring. Josephus's description of the ancient city wall runs past the spring of Siloam (War 5.145), so the tower may have belonged to the fortifications there. In 2004 Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron uncovered the steps of the large Second Temple period pool of Siloam, the pool of John 9:7, which shows that the district was busy in Jesus' day. Nothing in Josephus connects the collapse with Pilate's building works, and it may have been a simple accident. That is part of Jesus' point: the first report involves human cruelty, the second an event with no villain at all.

Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39, when the emperor Gaius (Caligula) exiled him to Gaul (Antiquities 18.240-256). He had already imprisoned and executed John the Baptist (3:19-20, 9:7-9; Antiquities 18.116-119). If Jesus was in Perea at this point on the road to Jerusalem, as many think, he was in Antipas's territory, and the threat was real. Interpreters differ over whether the Pharisees' warning (verse 31) was friendly or a ploy to move him on; Luke does not say, and his picture of the Pharisees is mixed (7:36, 11:37, 14:1; Acts 5:34-39). Jesus' charge that Jerusalem kills the prophets draws on Israel's own confession (Nehemiah 9:26) and on remembered cases: Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22), and Uriah son of Shemaiah was killed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20-23). The Lives of the Prophets, a Jewish collection from around the first century, says Jeremiah was stoned in Egypt (2:1).

Parallels to parts of the chapter appear in Matthew 13:31-33 and Mark 4:30-32 (mustard seed and leaven), Matthew 7:13-14 and 7:22-23 (the narrow gate and the rejected who claim acquaintance), Matthew 8:11-12 (many from east and west), Matthew 19:30 and 20:16 (first and last), and Matthew 23:37-39 (the lament over Jerusalem, placed there after Jesus has entered the city). The two reports of disaster, the fig tree parable, the healing of the bent woman, and the reply to Herod are found only in Luke. Luke also lacks the story of Jesus cursing a fig tree that Mark tells in the last week (Mark 11:12-14, 20-21), and many commentators think the parable here does in words what that sign does in Mark.
cultural:
Many in the ancient world, including some in Israel, assumed that sudden disaster revealed hidden sin. Job's friends argue this way (Job 4:7-8), the disciples ask whose sin caused a man's blindness (John 9:2), and a saying attributed to Rabbi Ammi in the Babylonian Talmud holds that there is no death without sin and no suffering without iniquity, though the Talmud goes on to refute it (b. Shabbat 55a). In verse 4 Jesus calls the eighteen opheiletai, literally ‘debtors’, using the language of debt for sin that also appears in Matthew's form of the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:12), a usage that reflects the Aramaic of the time.

Fig trees were often planted in vineyards, and a person sitting under his own vine and fig tree was a picture of peace (1 Kings 4:25, Micah 4:4). Israel was pictured as a vineyard or a fig tree from which God looked for fruit (Isaiah 5:1-7, Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10, Micah 7:1). The Law forbade eating the fruit of a newly planted tree for its first three years (Leviticus 19:23-25), so if the owner's three years are counted after that, the tree had been in the ground for six or seven. Digging around a tree and laying manure (kopria) around it was extraordinary care for a fig, which normally needed little. An ancient Near Eastern wisdom tale, the Story of Ahikar, attested in Aramaic from the fifth century BC at Elephantine in Egypt, has a fruitless tree by the water beg its master to move it and give it another chance, and the master refuses; Jesus' vinedresser wins the extension the tree in Ahikar does not.

Sabbath law defined work by listing labors, and the Mishnah's list of thirty-nine includes tying and untying knots (m. Shabbat 7:2). The rabbis nonetheless allowed a cow's rope to be tied to its trough on the Sabbath (m. Shabbat 15:2) and made provision for watering cattle at wells (m. Eruvin 2:1-4). The Damascus Document from Qumran was stricter, forbidding anyone to lift an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14). Jesus argues from the more lenient common practice his hearers followed. The synagogue leader (archisynagōgos) was a lay official who arranged services and readings; the Theodotus inscription, found by Raymond Weill in Jerusalem in 1913 and dated before AD 70, honors Theodotus son of Vettenus, priest and archisynagōgos, who built a synagogue for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments. The leader here does not rebuke Jesus directly but lectures the crowd, citing the command to work six days (Exodus 20:9, Deuteronomy 5:13).

The mustard seed was proverbially tiny. Pliny the Elder notes that once mustard is sown it is scarcely possible to rid the ground of it (Natural History 19.170-171), and the Mishnah classes mustard as a field crop not to be sown in a garden bed with vegetables (m. Kilayim 3:2). Luke's version, unlike Mark's, has it thrown into a garden (kēpos) and says it becomes a tree, and birds nesting in a tree's branches recall the great kingdoms of Daniel 4:12 and 4:21 and the cedar God plants in Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6. Leaven was sourdough, a lump of old fermented dough worked into new flour. It was removed from houses at Passover (Exodus 12:15) and could stand for corruption (Luke 12:1, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8), though leavened loaves were also offered to God (Leviticus 7:13, 23:17). The woman ‘hid’ (enekrupsen) it in three seahs of flour, together about an ephah, the amount Sarah baked for her three visitors (Genesis 18:6); estimates run to well over twenty liters, enough bread for a large gathering.

In a village the householder barred the door at night (11:7), and those outside were at his mercy. To say ‘I do not know where you are from’ disowns any relationship. Reclining at table in the kingdom with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob draws on the prophets' picture of a feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6-8) and of the scattered gathered from every direction (Psalm 107:3, Isaiah 49:12). In Jewish usage the fox stood for a small, cunning, destructive creature, not a noble one (Nehemiah 4:3, Song of Songs 2:15, Ezekiel 13:4), and a saying in the Mishnah advises being a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes (m. Avot 4:15). The mother bird sheltering her young is an old image for God's protection (Deuteronomy 32:11, Ruth 2:12, Psalm 17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 91:4).
literary:
The chapter alternates warning and good news. Two reports of disaster produce the same refrain twice, “unless you repent, you too will all perish” (verses 3 and 5), and the fig tree parable follows with an ending left open: the reader never learns whether the tree bears fruit. The healing story shows the kingdom breaking in, and the paired parables of mustard seed and leaven (18-21), one about a man and one about a woman in Luke's habit of pairing, describe its growth from small, hidden beginnings. A travel notice (verse 22) opens the second half. There a question about how many will be saved (verse 23) is turned back on the questioner, since Jesus answers in the plural, to everyone present, with a command to strive rather than a number. The chapter closes with a prophetic lament that quotes Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims' psalm that the crowds will shout as Jesus approaches the city (19:38).

Several threads tie the chapter together. The number eighteen appears three times, for the victims of the tower (verse 4) and for the years of the woman's bondage (verses 11 and 16), setting a death no one could prevent beside a bondage Jesus ends. The verbs of binding and loosing link the Sabbath healing to the Nazareth sermon, where Jesus announced release for the oppressed (4:18): the woman is ‘loosed’ (apolelusai, verse 12), and Jesus argues that people ‘loose’ (luei) their animals, so this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan ‘bound’ (edēsen), must be loosed from her ‘bond’ (desmos, verse 16). The necessity word dei runs through the chapter: the synagogue leader says there are six days on which it is necessary to work (verse 14), Jesus answers that it was necessary for this woman to be freed (verse 16), and he says it is necessary for him to go on his way (verse 33). Two uses of dei stand against one: human rules about necessary work, and God's necessity of release and of the road to Jerusalem.

The narrow door section (22-30) builds by reversal. Those who claim that Jesus ate and drank with them and taught in their streets are refused, while people from the four points of the compass recline with the patriarchs, and the section ends with a proverb that recurs in the Gospels in different settings: some who are last will be first. The closing unit (31-35) moves from a threat to a lament. Jesus' reply to Herod is built on a three-day pattern (today, tomorrow, the third day) repeated twice with different verbs, and the lament addresses Jerusalem directly with a doubled name, the form of David's grief over Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33) and of Jesus' address to Martha (10:41). It ends with a promise as well as a judgment: the house is abandoned, but a day is coming when the city will say, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.”

outline.t: Disasters and the call to repent
The parable of the barren fig tree
A crippled woman freed on the Sabbath
Herod the fox and the lament over Jerusalem

doctrines.note: Jesus turns news of disaster away from speculation about the victims and toward the hearers: “unless you repent, you too will all perish” (verses 3 and 5). The present subjunctive in the first saying (metanoēte) suggests an ongoing turning, and the fig tree parable adds that God's patience gives time for fruit but not unlimited time (verses 8-9).

Jesus twice denies that the victims of violence and accident were worse sinners than others (verses 2 and 4), refusing the simple equation of suffering with special guilt. The woman's disability is traced to Satan's binding (verse 16), not to her own sin, and Jesus treats her release as God's will for her.

The synagogue leader treats healing as work to be kept to the six days (verse 14). Jesus answers from the Sabbath's own purpose: if animals are loosed for water on that day, a daughter of Abraham must be loosed from Satan's bond on it (verses 15-16). The Sabbath, which remembered Israel's release from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15), is the fitting day for release.

The kingdom begins small and hidden, like a seed thrown into a garden or leaven hidden in flour, and grows until it shelters birds and leavens the whole batch (verses 18-21). It gathers people from east and west and north and south to recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (verses 28-29), and it reverses expectations of who will be inside.

The door of the master's house is shut, and those outside who claim acquaintance are sent away as evildoers in words from Psalm 6:8 (verses 25-27). The lament over Jerusalem announces that its house is abandoned (verse 35). Judgment in this chapter is real and final, yet it falls on refusal of an invitation that was long and patiently extended (verse 34).

words.note: Metanoeō, to repent, to change one's mind and direction. It occurs about 34 times in the New Testament, nine of them in Luke and twelve in Revelation. In the Greek of Luke's day it could describe a simple change of mind, but in the Gospels it carries the Hebrew sense of shuv, to turn or return to God. In verses 3 and 5 it is addressed to the hearers, not to the victims: the question is not what they did but what you will do.

Opheiletēs, debtor, one who owes. It occurs 7 times in the New Testament. In verse 4 Jesus asks whether the eighteen were greater ‘debtors’ than everyone else in Jerusalem, where the BSB renders the sense as more sinful. The use of debt language for sin reflects the Aramaic of Jesus' day (compare Matthew 6:12 with Luke 11:4) and prepares for the many debts and debtors in Luke's parables (7:41-43, 16:1-8).

Deō, to bind, tie. It occurs about 43 times in the New Testament, most often of physical binding and imprisonment, as of Paul in Acts. In verse 16 Satan has ‘bound’ the woman for eighteen years. Jesus sets the word against luō, to loose, and his exorcisms and healings elsewhere are pictured as binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29, compare Luke 11:21-22).

Luō, to loose, untie, release, and by extension to destroy or annul. It occurs about 42 times in the New Testament, seven of them in Luke. In verses 15 and 16 it is the heart of Jesus' argument: each of you ‘looses’ an ox or donkey on the Sabbath, so this woman must be ‘loosed’ from her bond. The related compound apoluō is used when Jesus tells her she is set free (verse 12).

Agōnizomai, to strive, struggle, contend, from agōn, a contest; the English agonize comes from it. It occurs 8 times in the New Testament, often of Christian effort (1 Corinthians 9:25, Colossians 1:29, 1 Timothy 6:12, 2 Timothy 4:7). In verse 24 the present imperative calls for sustained, earnest effort to enter while the door is open. Its sense is urgency and seriousness, not earning entry by merit, since the door is the master's and he alone opens or shuts it.

Thura, door. It occurs about 39 times in the New Testament, and three times in verses 24-25. Matthew's parallel speaks of a narrow gate (pulē) and a road (Matthew 7:13-14); Luke's image is a house door, which suits the banquet that follows (verses 28-29): the door opens onto a meal. Once the householder rises and shuts it, knocking does not open it, in contrast to the promise that the one who knocks will be answered (11:9-10) while the time of invitation lasts.

Teleioō, to complete, bring to its goal, perfect. It occurs about 23 times in the New Testament, nine in Hebrews, where it describes Christ made perfect through suffering (Hebrews 2:10, 5:9). In verse 32 the present passive teleioumai, ‘I am brought to completion’, is rendered ‘I will reach My goal’. The same verb is used of completing the days of a feast (2:43) and, in John 19:28-30, related forms mark the completion of Jesus' work on the cross, which is where his road ends.

Episunagō, to gather together. It occurs 8 times in the New Testament, all in the Synoptic Gospels. In verse 34 Jesus uses it of his longing to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her brood. In Mark 13:27 and Matthew 24:31 the same verb describes the Son of Man gathering his elect from the four winds, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for God's regathering of scattered Israel (for example Psalm 106:47, 2 Maccabees 1:27).

christ:
The chapter reveals Jesus as the one who frees the bound and gathers the scattered, and as the prophet who must die in Jerusalem. In the Sabbath healing he calls the woman, speaks a word of release, and lays hands on her, and she stands straight and glorifies God (verses 12-13). Luke calls him “the Lord” as he answers the synagogue leader (verse 15), and his argument claims that setting a daughter of Abraham free from Satan is what the Sabbath was for. The act fulfills the program he announced at Nazareth from Isaiah 61, release for captives and freedom for the oppressed (4:18), and it anticipates Peter's summary in Acts 10:38 that Jesus went about healing all who were oppressed by the devil.

His reply to Herod shows that no king controls his path. He will go on casting out demons and healing, and on the third day he will be brought to completion (verse 32). The phrase describes a short, set time, but in a Gospel where the Son of Man is to be raised on the third day (9:22, 18:33, 24:7, 24:46), readers have long heard in it a hint of the passion and resurrection. His word that it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem (verse 33) is grim irony, since John the Baptist was killed at Machaerus, but it names the city as the place where Israel's rejection of God's messengers will reach its climax, and Jesus goes there on purpose.

The lament over Jerusalem uses an image the Old Testament applies to God himself: sheltering under the wings (Deuteronomy 32:11, Ruth 2:12, Psalm 91:4). Jesus speaks of having longed ‘how often’ to gather Jerusalem's children, as if he had been the one sending the prophets all along, which is how Luke's Jesus also speaks of the Wisdom of God sending prophets and apostles (11:49). He stands where God stands in the story of Israel, and he grieves as God grieves. The longing, met with refusal, will end in tears as he approaches the city (19:41-44) and in the cross, where the scattered from east and west (verse 29) will be gathered by one who spreads out his arms. The quotation of Psalm 118:26 points both to his entry into the city (19:38) and beyond it, to a day when those who rejected him will welcome him, a hope Paul also holds out for Israel (Romans 11:25-27).
interpretation:
Early Christian preaching read the fig tree as humanity or Israel under God's patience. Augustine, in a sermon on this passage (Sermon 110), took the three years as the times before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, the digging around the tree as the teaching of humility and repentance, and the manure as the sinner's lowly penitence that makes the tree fruitful. The Puritan John Bunyan's treatise The Barren Fig-Tree applied the parable to the ‘fruitless professor’, the churchgoer whose life bears no fruit, and warned that the day of grace can end before life does.

The question of verse 23 has a long history of its own. In Jewish tradition the Mishnah teaches that all Israel has a share in the world to come, apart from named exceptions (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), while the apocalypse known as 4 Ezra, written around AD 100, has an angel tell Ezra that the Most High made this world for many but the world to come for few (4 Ezra 8:1-3). Among Christians, Augustine and Thomas Aquinas held that the saved are fewer than the lost; Aquinas argues that the vision of God so exceeds fallen nature that the elect are a minority, though only God knows their number (Summa Theologiae I q.23 a.7). John Calvin, commenting on the verse in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555), stressed that Jesus refuses to satisfy curiosity and turns the questioner to his own entry, rebuking those who look around to see who else is coming. Origen's hope for the restoration of all things and, in modern times, David Bentley Hart's That All Shall Be Saved (2019) take the opposite pole, reading judgment texts like this one as warnings rather than final numbers.

The opening verses have been preached after public disasters. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755, John Wesley's Serious Thoughts Occasioned by the Late Earthquake at Lisbon (1755) read the catastrophe as a summons to repentance, while Voltaire's Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756) attacked the optimism that found such deaths part of a good design. Modern commentators often cite Luke 13:1-5 on both sides of that argument. N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) reads ‘you too will all perish’ as a warning about Roman swords and falling masonry in the war of AD 66 to 70 if Israel kept to the road of violent revolt.

C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) read the mustard seed and leaven as announcing a kingdom already arriving in Jesus' ministry, and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus) called them parables of contrast between tiny beginnings and a great end. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) took leaven as always a symbol of evil and read the parable as a warning that false doctrine would permeate the professing church, a reading most commentators reject because Luke explicitly says the kingdom of God is like leaven. The hen of verse 34 gave medieval devotion one of its tenderest images: Anselm of Canterbury's Prayer to Saint Paul addresses Jesus as a mother who gathers her chicks under her wings, a strand of piety Caroline Walker Bynum traced in Jesus as Mother. On the Mount of Olives the church of Dominus Flevit, designed by Antonio Barluzzi and built between 1953 and 1955, has an altar mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.

In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C, 13:31-35 is read on the Second Sunday in Lent, 13:1-9 on the Third Sunday in Lent, and 13:10-17 in late August (Proper 16). The Roman lectionary reads 13:1-9 on the Third Sunday of Lent and 13:22-30 on the Twenty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year C.
text:
Three differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 35 the earliest witnesses, including P75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘your house is left to you’ without erēmos, ‘desolate’. Codex Bezae and the later Byzantine manuscripts add the word, probably from Matthew 23:38, and the King James Version has it. Several modern versions, the BSB among them, also print ‘desolate’, either following those manuscripts or making explicit what ‘left to you’ means in the light of Jeremiah 12:7 and 22:5. The meaning is much the same: God's presence has departed and the house is abandoned.

In the second half of verse 35 the manuscripts vary between ‘until you say’ and ‘until the time comes when you say’ (heōs hēxei hote eipēte), which the King James Version follows. In verse 19 the later manuscripts behind the King James Version say the mustard became ‘a great tree’, adding megas, which the earliest manuscripts lack; Matthew and Mark call it the greatest of garden plants. In verse 32 some manuscripts read epitelō for apotelō, a difference of prefix with no change of sense. None of these variants alters the meaning of the passage.

teach.big: The kingdom that frees the bound and welcomes the far-off is present in Jesus now, and because God's patience has a limit, the right response to every tragedy and every religious question is to repent and enter while the door is open.

outline.t: Disasters are not a measure of the victims' guilt; they are a summons to the survivors to turn to God.
God's patience is real and costly, like a gardener who digs and fertilizes, but it is time given for fruit, not a permanent reprieve.
Jesus sees, calls, and frees those who have been bent under long burdens, and he treats their release as the true purpose of the Sabbath.
The kingdom starts small and hidden and grows beyond all expectation; do not despise small beginnings.
The question is not how many will be saved but whether you will enter; familiarity with Jesus is not the same as knowing him.
Jesus walks toward his death on purpose, and his judgment on Jerusalem comes with tears and a longing to gather.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misuses recur. The first reads verses 1-5 backward, as if Jesus were saying that disaster is always punishment for someone's sin; he says the opposite about the victims and turns the warning on the living. A related misuse announces that a particular hurricane, epidemic, or attack was God's judgment on a particular group, which is exactly the move Jesus refuses. The second treats the fig tree as a promise of endless second chances, ignoring that the gardener asks for one more year. The third makes the bent woman's illness a sign of her personal sin or weak faith; Luke says she was bound by Satan and says nothing of her faith before Jesus calls her.

With the mustard seed and leaven, avoid turning them into a promise of steady numerical church growth, or reading leaven as evil when Jesus says the kingdom is like it. With the narrow door, avoid preaching either a numerical answer (few or many) that Jesus declines to give, or a message of anxious self-effort; the striving is urgent response to an open door, not earning a place, and the door belongs to the master. Avoid treating the Pharisees of verse 31 as uniformly villains, and avoid reading the lament over Jerusalem as a verdict against the Jewish people as such. Jesus grieves as a Jew over his own city in words drawn from Israel's own prophets, and the chapter ends with a future welcome, not a final rejection.
teach.pastoral: Verses 1-5 will press on anyone who has lost someone to violence, accident, or disaster, and on those who have been told, perhaps by other Christians, that their suffering was punishment. Let Jesus' ‘No, I tell you’ be heard clearly before the call to repentance. The healing of the bent woman will touch people living with chronic illness, disability, or long depression; Jesus sees her first and speaks to her before anyone asks, but do not imply that those who remain unhealed are less loved or less faithful. The narrow door can terrify the scrupulous, who fear they are among those shut out; point them to the master who opens, to the invitation still extended, and to Jesus' longing to gather in verse 34. For those grieving a city, a church, or a family that has refused God, the lament shows that tears are a faithful response.

hard.q: If the victims of Pilate and the tower were not worse sinners, why does Jesus say his hearers will perish unless they repent?
hard.a:
The objection comes from two sides. One older view, found in Job's friends and in the saying attributed to Rabbi Ammi that there is no death without sin (b. Shabbat 55a), holds that suffering does track guilt; on that view Jesus' denial is puzzling and his warning seems to reinstate what he denied. From the other side, skeptical readers since Voltaire's Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756) have asked how a good God can permit a tower to fall on eighteen people at all, and whether a call to repent is simply a way of changing the subject. Some modern readers hear the warning as the very thing Jesus rejected: disaster used as a threat.

Interpreters have answered in three main ways. Many read the warning as about final judgment. Death comes to all, and the sudden deaths of others remind the living that they too must meet God unprepared unless they turn now; Wesley's tract on the Lisbon earthquake (1755) applied the text this way. Others, including N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996), read it historically: the word homoiōs, ‘in the same way’, points to a specific fate. If Israel kept to the road of armed revolt against Rome, its people would die as the Galileans did, by Roman swords in the temple precincts, and as the eighteen did, under falling buildings, which is what happened in AD 70. Many commentators hold that both senses are present, since for Luke the fall of Jerusalem is itself a judgment that anticipates the last one (19:41-44, 21:20-24). On the skeptical question, Jesus does not offer a theory of why the tower fell. He refuses the moral arithmetic that makes the dead guilty and the survivors safe, and he redirects attention from explanation to response. The fig tree parable that follows is part of the answer: God's patience is real and is meant to lead to repentance (compare Romans 2:4), and in the next scene Jesus shows what God intends for those bound by suffering, which is release.

hard.q: Will only a few be saved?
hard.a:
The question is asked by someone in the crowd (verse 23), and it has been argued ever since. The strongest case for ‘few’ rests on this passage and its parallel (Matthew 7:13-14, where few find the road that leads to life), on the Jewish apocalypse 4 Ezra, which says the world to come was made for few (8:1-3), and on the long line of Christian theologians, including Augustine and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I q.23 a.7), who concluded that the elect are a minority. At the other pole, Origen hoped for the restoration of all things, and David Bentley Hart (That All Shall Be Saved, 2019) argues that a good Creator cannot finally lose any creature, so that texts like this are warnings rather than censuses. Jewish tradition in the Mishnah held that all Israel has a share in the world to come (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), and the skeptic Bertrand Russell, in his lecture Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), counted Jesus' teaching about exclusion and weeping and gnashing of teeth a defect in his moral character.

Jesus' own answer does not settle the number. He turns the question into a command addressed to all his hearers: strive to enter through the narrow door (verse 24). John Calvin, commenting on the verse (Harmony of the Gospels, 1555), saw in this a rebuke of curiosity that looks around to see who else is coming instead of entering. The passage does make some things plain. The door will be shut, and some who expect to be inside will not be (verses 25-28). Mere acquaintance with Jesus, having eaten in his company and heard him teach, is not the same as being known by him. And the company inside will be larger and more surprising than the questioner assumed, with people from east and west and north and south at table (verse 29). Christians who hold that few will be saved, those who hope that many or all will be, and those who hold that the number is simply not revealed all read this passage; what it requires of each of them is the same, to enter while the door is open. Questions about the fate of those who never heard and about universal salvation remain disputed among faithful Christians, and this passage alone does not resolve them.

observe: What two events do people report or recall in verses 1-5, and what does Jesus say twice about each?
List the verbs of binding and loosing in verses 12-16. Who binds, who looses, and what is loosed?
In verses 25-27, what do those outside the door claim, and how does the master answer them?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus answers the question ‘will only a few people be saved?’ with a command rather than a number?
What does the fig tree parable add to the call to repent in verses 1-5? What does the gardener's request reveal?
How does the image of the hen gathering her chicks (verse 34) shape the way we should hear the judgment announced in verse 35?
apply: When you hear of a disaster, do you tend to look for someone to blame, or to feel safe because it happened to others? How does Jesus redirect that instinct?
The kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed. Where might God be doing something small in your life or community that you have been tempted to overlook?
Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem, but it was unwilling. Where are you resisting being gathered, and what would it mean to stop?
